sm: Sweeping outages, including at the National Security Agency and Apple, have sparked fears of coordinated cyber attacks, though officials insist things are not what they seem. One official says with complete certainty that the country is not under attack and that the homeland is very secure. Hosts John Bickley and Georgia Howe open the Wednesday, November 18th edition. Also ahead are President Trump's announcement of a major Alaska energy project to export record amounts of affordable American energy, and new civil rights investigations into over a dozen colleges over DEI in teacher training.

The NSA is the latest to be hit by a series of outages sweeping the country, this time affecting a classified communication network. Former cyber criminal turned security consultant Brett Johnson says Microsoft, the FAA, banks, airlines and the NSA have all been affected, which is worrying. But there is no established evidence of coordinated attacks, which he finds almost more concerning, since ordinary failures cause this much disruption. He says AI did not invent cyber crime but industrializes it, while imperfect AI installs and holiday website updates can also cause outages and bot-driven inventory grabs.

Johnson explains that attacks have three motivations: status, cash and ideology, and the targets hit have hallmarks of ideological attacks. Still, he says he would be more worried if systems stayed down longer or if someone claimed responsibility, since attackers usually want credit to instill fear. On AI defense, he says the bad guys are winning because defenders are reactive and AI learns only from successful attacks. He hopes that changes in 18 to 24 months, noting cyber crime is a ten trillion dollar economy. The hosts say people are understandably worried.

President Trump began a three-day Asia trip by announcing approval of a deal for the long-stalled Alaska LNG project, speaking at a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders in the Philippines. The pipeline would carry gas from the North Slope more than 800 miles to the Kenai Peninsula for processing and export. Cabot Phillips says the idea has floated for decades, with federal permitting finished last year. Trump credited a historic South Korean investment, which the White House says could reach 54 billion dollars, though details remain under review.

Phillips says the biggest global impact is energy security for allies like Japan, Australia and South Korea, which were hit by price spikes when the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted in April. Energy Secretary Chris Wright called it probably the most important energy infrastructure project of this administration. Taiwan will buy 30 percent of the gas for 20 years and invest up to 4.4 billion dollars. Alaska also approved a 50-year lease for a North Slope data center that would run on local gas and employ about 1,500 during construction.

On the trip, Trump met leaders of Japan, India and Australia in the Philippines and signed critical minerals deals meant to reduce dependence on China. He announced a multi-year trade deal with Thailand to drop tariffs on American exports, plus a joint exercise and an AI accelerator. He then arrived in Shenzhen, China for the APEC summit, where on Thursday he is expected to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin to discuss trade, denuclearization and wars.

The Trump administration has opened civil rights investigations into teacher training programs over alleged preferential treatment based on race or sex. Bill Jacobson of the Equal Protection Project says the Education Department opened 15 investigations, 12 from his group's complaints. He says programs in several states, including Minnesota, offer significant money to non-whites to become teachers. Schools flagged include Drake University, UCLA, College of DuPage, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville and Middle Tennessee State University. He says outreach is fine, but money or entry limited by race is unlawful, and the schools are simply asked to follow their own non-discrimination policies.

Jacobson says the 2023 Supreme Court affirmative action ruling rests on the Equal Protection Clause and Civil Rights Act, so it applies equally to scholarships and teacher pipelines. Race gets the strictest scrutiny and racial balancing is not a legitimate interest. On threats to funding and tax-exempt status, he says the government would have to show discrimination goes to the core of an institution, as in the Bob Jones case. He considers losing federal funding for noncompliance with civil rights laws a greater threat than losing tax exemption, and the hosts note universities pay attention to funding.
